text: This lesson is about a real limitation of the plain JOIN you've used your entire career, and the two different keywords different platforms invented to fix it. The good news up front: the underlying concept is fully portable. Only the spelling changes depending on which dialect you're in — and by the end of this lesson you'll know all of them.

Here's the limitation. A plain JOIN's right-hand side — a table, a view, a derived subquery — gets evaluated completely independently. It has no idea what's happening in the rest of the FROM clause. That's fine for joining two ordinary tables, but it falls apart the moment you want something like 'for each customer, give me their three most recent orders.' The subquery that finds those three orders needs to know WHICH customer it's filtering for, on a row-by-row basis — and a plain JOIN simply can't pass that information in. Try it, and you get an error: the customer column isn't in scope inside that subquery.

T-SQL's answer is CROSS APPLY. Customers, CROSS APPLY, select top 3 order id and order date from Orders where Orders dot CustomerID equals c dot CustomerID, order by order date descending. CROSS APPLY lets that derived table reach back and see columns from every table that comes before it in the FROM clause — exactly the missing piece. And just like a regular join, there's an inner and outer variant: CROSS APPLY drops a customer with zero orders entirely, the same way an inner join would; OUTER APPLY keeps that customer in the results with nulls in the applied columns, the same way a left join would.

PostgreSQL has had the identical capability for years, and MySQL caught up in version 8.0.14 — both call it LATERAL instead of APPLY. Customers, CROSS JOIN LATERAL, the same correlated subquery, limit 3 instead of top 3. Same correlation, same result, different keyword, combined with JOIN rather than standing alone. If you can write CROSS APPLY in T-SQL, you already understand CROSS JOIN LATERAL in PostgreSQL and MySQL — there is nothing new to learn conceptually, just a different word to type.

Oracle is the interesting case: it supports BOTH spellings. Oracle added LATERAL support back in version 12c. Then, in a later 12c release, Oracle added its OWN CROSS APPLY and OUTER APPLY syntax too — and the reason is telling: Oracle added it specifically to make migrating T-SQL code over from SQL Server easier. That's a strong signal about how portable this concept really is: even Oracle's own engineering team decided it was worth adding T-SQL's exact keyword as an alias.

So here's the map to carry forward: T-SQL uses CROSS APPLY and OUTER APPLY. PostgreSQL and MySQL 8.0.14-plus use CROSS JOIN LATERAL and LEFT JOIN LATERAL. Oracle 12c-plus accepts either spelling. The concept — a derived table correlated to an earlier table in the same query — is identical everywhere; only the keyword changes. Next lesson, we look at something even MORE consistent across dialects: common table expressions, the WITH clause, which is remarkably uniform across every platform in this course.
